title: Rockingham County v. Luten Bridge Co.
summary: After receiving the county’s repudiation, a bridge builder could recover its legitimate breach losses but could not enlarge recovery by continuing to build a bridge the county no longer wanted.
notes: The editors explain that a failure to mitigate generally limits damages rather than creating independent liability to the breaching party. The notes raise uncertainty about repudiation and contrast a performance-only offer under Restatement § 45; those textbook problems remain questions rather than decided extensions of this holding.

sections.Parties: Luten Bridge Company was the contractor. Rockingham County, acting through its commissioners, was the contracting public body that repudiated the bridge project.
sections.Material Facts: The county’s board entered a bridge-construction contract on January 7, 1924. Considerable opposition followed. On February 21 the county told Luten not to continue and refused to recognize its contractual obligation. Luten had then spent about $1,900 on labor and materials. Despite the notice, it continued construction and sought payment for the resulting work. The county also abandoned the road of which the bridge was to form a part, leaving the completed bridge in the forest without value to the county’s project.
sections.Procedural History: The district court directed a verdict for Luten for the amount it claimed for the work. The Fourth Circuit reversed in 1929. Its damages discussion accepts that the county’s attempted cancellation was wrongful; the dispute concerns the consequences of the builder’s continued performance.
sections.Issue: Can a nonbreaching builder continue work after an unequivocal repudiation and charge the breaching owner for the resulting avoidable expense?
sections.Holding: No. Luten should have stopped after receiving the county’s notice and claimed its recoverable losses, including the profit it would have earned. It could not recover added costs incurred by completing the unwanted bridge.
sections.Reasoning:
The county’s power to avoid additional liability for waste did not give it a legal right to cancel without compensation. Its notice was a breach. But damages aim to compensate the builder for the injury caused by that breach, and a builder cannot increase the injury unnecessarily after learning that performance will not be accepted or paid for. An award protecting the builder’s profit and legitimate losses can preserve its economic expectation while freeing its resources for other uses.

The example was particularly stark because the county abandoned the connecting road. Continued work produced a useless bridge and enlarged costs without delivering the benefit the project had contemplated. The court applied avoidability to those post-notice expenditures, rather than treating every expense following breach as automatically recoverable.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Luten Bridge introduces mitigation as a limit on recovery. It also distinguishes the wrongfulness of repudiation from the injured party’s response to it.

topics.remedies: Excludes losses reasonably avoidable by stopping work after repudiation.
topics.mitigation: Shows why post-notice performance costs differ from protected profit and unavoidable loss.
topics.repudiation: The county’s wrongful refusal supplied the notice that made continued expenditure avoidable.

mnemonic.rationale: A bridge to nowhere, finished anyway
